responses_by_run.answer: Athena turned Arachne into a spider as punishment for her pride and defiance [1]. Arachne was an extraordinarily skilled weaver who refused to acknowledge that her talent came from Athena's instruction [1]. When Athena challenged her to a weaving contest in disguise, Arachne insulted the goddess and refused to apologize, declaring she would compete against the goddess herself [1]. After Athena revealed herself and they completed their contest, Athena found Arachne's work flawless but was enraged by the girl's skill and defiance [2]. Athena destroyed Arachne's web and struck her repeatedly [2]. When Arachne attempted to hang herself in despair, Athena saved her life but pronounced a cruel eternal punishment: she transformed Arachne into a spider, condemning her to dangle on a cord forever and to weave endlessly as a spider, so that her punishment would last throughout all generations [3].

Prometheus was punished for two related offenses. First, he stole fire and gave it to humans [1]. According to Apollodorus, Prometheus hid fire in a stalk of fennel and gave it to men, and when Zeus learned of this theft, he ordered Hephaestus to nail Prometheus to Mount Caucasus as punishment [1]. Second, Hesiod indicates that Prometheus was also punished for attempting to deceive Zeus by dividing portions of an ox unfairly during a dispute between gods and mortals at Mecone [2]. His punishment consisted of being bound with inextricable chains to a mountain, where an eagle devoured his liver daily, which would regenerate each night [3].

responses_by_run.answer: Odysseus escaped Polyphemus through two key actions. First, he blinded the Cyclops by sharpening a wooden club, heating it in fire, and driving it into Polyphemus's eye with the help of his comrades [1][2]. When Polyphemus called out to other Cyclopes for help, they misunderstood his cries of "Nobody" and departed [1]. Second, after the blinding, Odysseus tied the sheep together in groups of three and had his men cling to the undersides of the larger rams [3][4]. He himself grasped the largest ram and clung to its belly as the flocks were let out to pasture [3][4]. In this way, he and his surviving comrades escaped the cave hidden beneath the sheep and made their way to the ships [3][4].

At the wedding of Peleus and Thetis, the gods celebrated the marriage with feast and song on Mount Pelion [1]. The marriage took place after Peleus seized Thetis despite her shape-shifting resistance, holding her fast as she transformed into fire, water, and various beasts until she resumed her true form [1]. As wedding gifts, Chiron gave Peleus an ashen spear [1], and Poseidon gave him immortal horses named Balius and Xanthus [1].

Demeter stopped the crops from growing because she was grieving over the abduction of her daughter [1]. She vowed that she would never let fruit spring out of the ground until she beheld her own fair-faced daughter with her eyes [2].

responses_by_run.answer: Achilles withdrew from the fighting after his quarrel with Agamemnon because Agamemnon took his prize, Briseis. According to Homer's account, Achilles was angry that Agamemnon threatened to seize his war prize despite Achilles bearing the brunt of the fierce battle, while Agamemnon's own prize was far greater [1]. Achilles declared he would return home to Phthia rather than remain dishonored and pile up riches for Agamemnon [1]. Apollodorus's account more simply states that Achilles did not go forth to war because he was angry on account of Briseis, the daughter of the priest Chryses [2].

Athena turned Arachne into a spider as punishment for her pride and defiance [1]. Arachne was a mortal weaver of extraordinary skill who refused to acknowledge Athena's superiority in the art of weaving [1]. When Athena, disguised as an old woman, advised Arachne to show respect to the goddess, Arachne scornfully rejected the advice and challenged Athena herself to a weaving contest [1]. After Athena won the contest and destroyed Arachne's web—which depicted the gods' shameful deeds—she struck Arachne repeatedly on the head [1]. Arachne then attempted to hang herself, but Athena saved her life while pronouncing a curse: 'your fate shall be to dangle on a cord, and your posterity forever shall take your example, that your punishment may last forever!' [2]. Athena then sprinkled Arachne with magical herbs, causing her body to shrink and transform into a spider, condemned to weave webs eternally as an endless punishment for her presumption [3].

Prometheus was punished for multiple transgressions. He stole fire and gave it to humans [1], hiding the fire in a stalk of fennel [1]. Additionally, Prometheus attempted to deceive Zeus by dividing portions of an ox unfairly during a dispute between gods and mortals at Mecone, setting aside bones covered with fat for Zeus while giving the flesh to mortals [2]. Prometheus also 'matched himself in wit with the almighty son of Cronos,' which further provoked Zeus's anger [3]. As punishment, Zeus ordered Hephaestus to nail Prometheus to Mount Caucasus [1], and an eagle was set upon him to devour his liver daily, which would regenerate each night [2].

Odysseus escaped Polyphemus through a two-part plan. First, he blinded the Cyclops by sharpening a wooden club, heating it in fire, and driving it into Polyphemus's eye with the help of his comrades [1][2]. When Polyphemus called out to other Cyclopes for help, they misunderstood his cries of "Nobody" and departed [1][2]. Second, after the blinded Cyclops opened the cave door to let his flocks out to pasture, Odysseus tied the sheep together in groups of three and hid himself beneath the largest ram by clinging to its fleece [1][2]. He and his comrades escaped with the flocks to their ships and sailed away [1][2].

    JOIN relationships r ON (r.from_id = encounters.id OR r.to_id = encounters.id)

      AND encounters.depth < 20
